title: Kristin Harila: The Triple Crown
excerpt: In the 2026 season the Norwegian climber completed the Everest Triple Crown, a feat only four people had achieved before her, and no woman. Beneath the sporting achievement lies a story of loss, one mountain in October, and the real reason she came back.
seoTitle: Kristin Harila Completes the Everest Triple Crown

content.value: On the morning of 27 May 2026, Kristin Harila stood on the summit of Everest at 8,849 meters, the highest point on Earth. With that ascent she completed the Everest Triple Crown, Nuptse, Lhotse and Everest, the three highest peaks of the Everest massif, in a single climbing season. Only four people in history had done this before her, and no woman had ever been among them.
But to understand why this achievement matters so much, not just for Harila but for everyone who loves mountains, you have to go back three years, to a different mountain, and to one day in October.
Who is Kristin Harila

Kristin Harila became a household name in the climbing world in the summer of 2023. That year she and her climbing partner, the Nepali Sherpa climber Tenzing Lama Sherpa, summited all 14 mountains in the world above 8,000 meters in just 92 days.

It was a world record. It took the title from the climbers who had come before her and placed her at the forefront of high-altitude mountaineering. It is important to understand what the record involved and what it did not: the pair flew by helicopter between the base camps of different mountains and used supplemental oxygen on the summit pushes. It was an extraordinary logistical and physical undertaking of a new kind, fast, planned and supported. The record brought Harila worldwide fame, alongside criticism and controversy about the culture of record-chasing that has developed around the high mountains.
But the true story of Harila cannot be told through numbers. It begins with one person.
The brother lost on the mountain

Tenzing Lama Sherpa was not simply a business partner or a hired guide. Harila wrote after his death that he had been like a brother to her, that he embodied the very definition of human kindness, that on the mountain he moved as though he were part of it, and that he had generously invited her into that world.

Tenzing was an exceptionally gifted Nepali climber. He was the 50th person in history to summit all 14 eight-thousanders, and the 92-day record carried his name alongside Harila's. He had a family: a wife and two sons.

On 7 October 2023, less than three months after the pair completed their world record, Tenzing went to climb Shishapangma, one of the 14 eight-thousanders, in Tibet. A massive avalanche swept the main climbing route. Four climbers died that day. The bodies of two of them, including Tenzing, were never found.

The disaster on Shishapangma sharpened a debate already running in the climbing world: whether the pursuit of records pushes climbers into risks they should never have taken. Reports suggested some climbers on the mountain that day continued toward the summit even after a first avalanche. That question remains open, and painful.

For Harila, the loss was not theoretical. When the news came she flew immediately to Kathmandu. In the months that followed she did not try to move on as if nothing had happened. She tried to bring Tenzing home. She raised funds to finance a body recovery mission and even sold the watch that had accompanied her on the record expedition. Tenzing's wife and two sons asked for one thing: that his body be returned, so they could say goodbye.

That mission was blocked not by the mountain but by politics. Access to Shishapangma, on the Tibetan side, depends on Chinese permits, and they were not granted. Harila was forced to postpone the search again and again.

content.caption: Shishapangma, the Tibetan eight-thousander where Tenzing Lama Sherpa died in October 2023

content.value: When she set the mountains aside

A loss like that leaves its mark. In the period after Tenzing's death, Harila stepped back from climbing. She spoke openly about considering leaving the sport altogether. For someone whose record had been built on one close partnership, a partnership that death cut short, the mountain no longer looked the same.

Anyone who follows the climbing world knows this is not rare. Many of the best climbers reach a moment when they ask themselves whether the price is worth it. Some leave. Some return. Harila, in the end, came back, but differently.
The return: a farewell to Everest

When Harila announced her return to the Himalaya in 2026, she did not present it as another record chase. She described this challenge as her farewell to Everest: a last chance to stand before the highest mountain in the world on her own terms, and then let it go.

The return is connected to Tenzing in two ways. First, Harila said one of her goals on returning is to renew the attempt to reach Shishapangma and search for his body. Second, the very decision to return to the mountains, the place where she lost him, is a way of carrying his memory forward, into the mountains he loved.
The 2026 challenge is not only a sporting chapter. It is the journey of a person trying to close a circle.
What is the Everest Triple Crown

The challenge Harila chose is called the Everest Triple Crown. The concept is simple to define and nearly impossible to complete: climbing the three highest summits of the Everest massif in a single season.
Nuptse, 7,861 meters
The steep and technically demanding neighbor of Everest, a peak considered difficult even for experienced climbers. Harila summited Nuptse on 17 May 2026, without supplemental oxygen.

content.alt: Kristin Harila on the summit of Nuptse holding the Norwegian flag
content.caption: Kristin Harila on the summit of Nuptse, 17 May 2026. 7,861 meters, without supplemental oxygen

content.value: Lhotse, 8,516 meters
The fourth highest mountain in the world, adjacent to Everest and sharing part of its route. Harila summited Lhotse on 21 May 2026.

content.alt: Kristin Harila kneeling on the snowy summit of Lhotse with the Norwegian flag
content.caption: Kristin Harila on the summit of Lhotse, 21 May 2026. 8,516 meters

content.value: Everest, 8,849 meters
The highest point on Earth.

The difficulty is not only about altitude. It is cumulative. Three summit pushes to extreme altitude within one weather window, without the body ever truly recovering between them, is a load that very few people can bear. Only four climbers in history completed the Triple Crown before Harila, and no woman had ever been among them.

Harila completed the sequence within roughly ten days: Nuptse on 17 May, Lhotse on 21 May and Everest on 27 May. One important clarification: the original plan was to climb all three peaks without supplemental oxygen. Nuptse and Everest were done without oxygen, but according to a report by The Tourism Times citing the expedition manager, Harila used oxygen on Lhotse. The Triple Crown was completed, though not in the full no-oxygen version originally planned.

content.alt: Kristin Harila on the summit of Everest holding a Mt. Everest Spring 2026 sign
content.caption: Kristin Harila on the summit of Everest, 27 May 2026. 8,849 meters, completing the Triple Crown

content.value: Why without oxygen
The most significant decision in Harila's challenge is not the choice of mountains. It is the decision to go without oxygen.

At altitudes above 8,000 meters, in the zone climbers call the death zone, the amount of oxygen in every breath drops to roughly a third of what it is at sea level. The human body in that zone is failing: it consumes itself faster than it can recover. Most climbers who summit Lhotse and Everest do so with an oxygen mask, and this is not a luxury but a safety tool that dramatically reduces the risk of permanent physical damage.

content.title: ✦ The death zone
content.value: Altitude above 8,000 meters, where there is not enough oxygen in the air to sustain human life for any extended period. The body begins consuming muscle tissue to keep functioning. Every hour spent at this altitude carries a cost.
Climbing the Triple Crown without oxygen means doubling the difficulty and the risk at once.

The decision also drew criticism. Critics noted that despite the 14 eight-thousanders record, Harila had relatively limited experience climbing at extreme altitude without oxygen, since she used it on that record. Harila replied that her fast climbing style often left her climbing without oxygen in practice, and that as an athlete she was curious to know how her body would respond.
It all started on one mountain
There is one detail in Harila's story that is easy to miss, and it may be the most important of all for anyone reading these lines while thinking about their own first mountain.

Harila's first ascent to real altitude was not an eight-thousander. It was Lobuche, a peak in the Everest region at about 6,100 meters. That was in 2019. Harila described that climb as hard, a real effort. Six years later, the same woman climbs that same mountain in under three hours.

This is not a story about rare talent. It is a story about a journey. Every climber you see today on the world's summits, Kristin Harila included, started once, on one mountain, not yet knowing if they were capable. Lobuche is exactly that kind of mountain: a trekking peak above the Everest Base Camp trail and a first step into technical climbing in the Himalaya.

content.value: The mountain gives, and the mountain takes

Kristin Harila's story refuses to fit in the box of a records piece. It contains a rare athletic achievement, but it also holds deep loss, loyalty to a friend who is gone, and an honest question about the price of big dreams. That, perhaps, is the real story of the high mountains: they give a person a sense of being alive that is hard to find anywhere else, and they also know how to take.

At HighAir Expeditions we believe the journey to the mountain is not only about the summit. It is about the people beside you, the meaning you find along the way, and what you bring home. A portion of the proceeds from every expedition we run is dedicated to supporting cancer patients, because the mountains, in our view, are also a way of giving back.

content.value: Frequently asked questions
What is the Everest Triple Crown?

Climbing the three highest summits of the Everest massif in a single season: Nuptse (7,861 meters), Lhotse (8,516 meters) and Everest (8,849 meters). Only four people in history completed this sequence before Kristin Harila.
Has Kristin Harila completed the Everest Triple Crown?

Yes. On 27 May 2026 Harila summited Everest and became the first woman in history to complete the Triple Crown. Nuptse and Everest were climbed without supplemental oxygen; on Lhotse, according to reports citing the expedition manager, she used oxygen, so the challenge was not completed in the fully oxygen-free version originally planned.
Who was Tenzing Lama Sherpa?

A Nepali Sherpa climber and Harila's partner in the 2023 world record for climbing all 14 eight-thousanders. He died in an avalanche on Shishapangma in October 2023, and his body has never been found.
What was Harila's 14 peaks record?
In 2023, Harila and Tenzing Lama Sherpa summited all 14 mountains above 8,000 meters in 92 days, a world record. That ascent included the use of supplemental oxygen.
Why is climbing without oxygen considered so difficult?

At high altitude the amount of oxygen in every breath drops dramatically. Above 8,000 meters the body cannot recover. Doing without supplemental oxygen significantly increases both the effort and the risk, and is the domain of elite climbers.
